claims.text: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni is a single-phase FCC alloy.
The equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after comparable thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing will produce similar grain size and phase homogeneity across the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni has a greater degree of local chemical short-range order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Alloys with fewer constituents have less-pronounced short-range order than the quinary alloy.
Local chemical short-range order increases lattice distortion.
Short-range-ordered regions create heterogeneous dislocation-pinning sites.
Chemical short-range order produces rugged, non-uniform dislocation-line morphologies.
Short-range order increases resistance to deformation and dislocation glide.
Rugged, pinned dislocation paths raise the barrier to dislocation glide.
Under the controlled conditions, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni will have a higher yield stress than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Under the controlled conditions, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni will have a greater work-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The predicted yield-strength and work-hardening advantages are caused by the quinary alloy's greater short-range order and associated rugged dislocation morphology.
Processing deviations or phase separation could confound the inferred relationship between short-range order and dislocation behavior.
Atom-probe tomography or high-resolution TEM can quantify local short-range order, while in situ TEM can quantify dislocation-line ruggedness during deformation.
